description: Early blight is a prevalent fungal disease affecting tomatoes, potatoes, and other solanaceous crops. It causes significant foliage loss, fruit damage, and reduced yield if left unmanaged.
symptoms: Circular brown to dark brown spots with characteristic concentric rings (target board pattern) on older lower leaves.
Surrounding yellow halo (chlorosis) around dark spots.
Stem lesions that become elongated and sunken (collar rot in seedlings).
Sunken, leathery dark lesions on fruit near the stem end.
causes: Fungal pathogen Alternaria solani surviving in infected crop debris or volunteer plants.
Spore dissemination through wind, rain splashes, irrigation water, and farming tools.
contributing_conditions: Warm temperatures between 24°C and 29°C (75°F - 85°F).
High humidity and prolonged leaf wetness (frequent rain, heavy dew, or overhead irrigation).
Plant stress due to heavy fruit load or nutrient deficiency (especially nitrogen).
immediate_steps: Immediately prune and remove infected lower leaves using clean, sanitized pruning shears.
Do not compost infected plant parts; destroy or bury them away from fields.
Switch immediately from overhead sprinkling to drip or furrow irrigation to keep foliage dry.
organic_cultural_management: Apply organic copper fungicide or Bacillus subtilis biopesticide at early onset.
Spread organic straw mulch around plant bases to prevent soil-borne spores from splashing onto lower leaves.
Improve spacing between tomato rows to enhance air circulation and sun exposure.
prevention_methods: Practice 3-4 year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops (such as corn, beans, or grains).
Plant certified disease-free seeds and blight-resistant tomato cultivars.
Stake and cage plants to elevate foliage off moist soil.
safe_handling_precautions: Avoid handling or pruning tomato plants when leaves are wet with morning dew or rain.
Clean boots and sanitize tools with a 10% bleach solution between rows.
when_to_seek_expert: Consult your local Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or extension officer if defoliation exceeds 25% of canopy or fruit lesions begin spreading rapidly across the field.

description: Late blight is one of the most destructive agricultural diseases in history, capable of wiping out entire tomato and potato fields within a few days under damp, cool conditions.
symptoms: Water-soaked, pale greenish-grey irregular lesions on leaves that rapidly turn dark brown or purplish-black.
Delicate white fuzzy or cottony fungal growth on the underside of leaves during humid mornings.
Dark brown to black lesions on stems and petioles causing vine collapse.
Firm, rough, greasy golden-brown patches on green and ripe tomato fruits.
causes: Phytophthora infestans pathogen transported across long distances by wind-blown sporangia.
Overwinters in cull piles, volunteer potato tubers, and infected greenhouse seedlings.
contributing_conditions: Cool to moderate temperatures (15°C to 22°C).
Relative humidity consistently above 90% with extended periods of rain, fog, or persistent mist.
immediate_steps: Promptly isolate the infected area; remove and bag entire heavily infected plants to stop airborne spore release.
Stop all overhead irrigation immediately.
Notify neighboring farmers and agricultural extension officers due to severe risk of rapid regional outbreak.
organic_cultural_management: Apply approved copper hydroxide or copper octanoate formulations as protective barriers before wet weather fronts.
Ensure wide plant spacing and north-south row orientation for maximum sunlight penetration.
prevention_methods: Select late-blight-tolerant or resistant cultivars (e.g., Mountain Magic, Defiant PHR).
Destroy all volunteer potato and tomato plants and eliminate cull piles.
Monitor local university and government agricultural blight alert forecasts.
safe_handling_precautions: Dispose of infected plant tissues in sealed plastic bags or deep bury them; never leave them exposed on field borders.
Wash clothing and sanitize equipment before moving to unaffected fields.
when_to_seek_expert: Seek immediate emergency assistance from your agricultural university extension or horticulture officer immediately upon first suspicion.

description: Bacterial spot is a widespread bacterial affliction affecting foliage, stems, and fruits of tomatoes and peppers, causing severe defoliation and unmarketable blemished fruit.
symptoms: Small, angular, dark brown to black water-soaked spots (1-3 mm) on foliage.
Leaf spots may tear or drop out, giving leaves a shot-hole or ragged appearance.
Severe yellowing and dropping of heavily infected foliage.
Raised, scab-like blister spots on green fruit with dark brown borders.
causes: Seed-borne bacteria Xanthomonas species.
Transmitted via splashing rain, overhead irrigation, farm equipment, and workers.
contributing_conditions: High temperatures between 25°C and 30°C.
Heavy driving rains, storms, and prolonged foliage wetness.
immediate_steps: Cease overhead irrigation immediately.
Avoid working in field rows while plants are wet to prevent mechanical transmission.
organic_cultural_management: Apply copper bactericides combined with mancozeb or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens according to local extension advice.
Mulch soil around beds to prevent rainwater backsplashes.
prevention_methods: Use certified disease-free seeds or hot-water-treated seed stock (50°C for 25 minutes).
Rotate with non-host crops like corn, sorghum, or pulses for at least 2 seasons.
safe_handling_precautions: Disinfect pruning knives, shears, and stakes using 70% isopropyl alcohol or 10% sodium hypochlorite.
when_to_seek_expert: Consult extension specialists if copper-resistant bacterial strains are suspected in your district.

description: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) is an insect-transmitted virus causing severe stunting, leaf chlorosis, and dramatic flower drop resulting in zero fruit yield if contracted early.
symptoms: Severe upward curling and cupping of leaflets.
Marked yellowing (chlorosis) along leaflet margins and interveinal areas.
Bushy, stunted plant stature with shortened internodes.
Flower abortion and failure to set fruit; existing fruit remains small and pale.
causes: Transmitted exclusively by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci).
Not seed-borne or mechanically transmitted through touch.
contributing_conditions: Hot, dry weather favorable to rapid whitefly population explosions.
Presence of alternative weed hosts (nightshades, mallows) near tomato fields.
immediate_steps: Rogue out and destroy infected viral plants immediately by pulling and burying them.
Deploy yellow sticky traps across the plot (1 trap every 10-15 meters) to capture and monitor whitefly populations.
organic_cultural_management: Apply neem seed kernel extract (NSKE 5%) or horticultural insecticidal soaps to suppress nymphal whiteflies.
Use silver or reflective plastic mulch to disorient whiteflies and repel them from young plants.
prevention_methods: Grow TYLCV-resistant hybrid tomato varieties.
Raise seedlings under 40-50 mesh insect-proof nylon nets in nursery beds.
Eradicate weed hosts surrounding fields.
safe_handling_precautions: Always inspect underside of nursery seedling leaves for whitefly eggs before transplanting.
when_to_seek_expert: Consult your agricultural officer for regional integrated pest management (IPM) guidelines on vector resistance.

description: The tomato plant shows vigorous green foliage, normal leaf morphology, and no visible symptoms of fungal, bacterial, or viral disease.
symptoms: Lush, uniformly green compound leaves without spots, yellowing, or curling.
Sturdy erect stems with healthy trichomes (hairs).
Regular floral cluster development and healthy fruit set.
causes: Balanced soil nutrition, optimal watering, and proactive pest monitoring.
contributing_conditions: Well-drained loamy soil with pH 6.0 - 6.8.
Consistent moisture and 6-8 hours of direct daily sunlight.
immediate_steps: Maintain regular scheduled drip irrigation at root level.
Continue routine bi-weekly field scouting for early signs of pests.
organic_cultural_management: Apply balanced organic compost and vermicompost around root zones.
Prune non-fruiting suckers to focus plant energy on primary fruit clusters.
prevention_methods: Maintain weed-free borders.
Practice prophylactic neem oil spray every 14 days.
safe_handling_precautions: Store tools cleanly and maintain proper field sanitation.
when_to_seek_expert: No intervention required. Keep monitoring periodically.

description: Early blight is a recurring fungal leaf spot disease of potatoes that causes premature foliage senescence and surface lesions on tubers.
symptoms: Circular to angular brown spots on lower leaves with characteristic concentric ridges.
Yellowing around lesions followed by dry, brittle leaf drop.
Tubers develop dark, sunken, corky circular depressions with raised purplish margins.
causes: Alternaria solani fungus surviving in volunteer potatoes and solanaceous crop residues.
contributing_conditions: Alternating dry weather and humid/wet periods.
Nutrient-deficient soils (especially low potassium or low nitrogen).
immediate_steps: Remove heavily spotted lower leaves where practical in small plots.
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation during late afternoon or evening.
organic_cultural_management: Apply copper-based fungicides or Trichoderma harzianum bio-agent at first spot appearance.
Ensure adequate balanced fertilization to prevent premature crop stress.
prevention_methods: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers.
Follow crop rotation with legumes, maize, or pasture grasses.
Hill up soil around potatoes adequately to shield tubers from spore wash.
safe_handling_precautions: Allow tubers to fully cure in soil 10-14 days after vine kill before harvesting to prevent skin damage.
when_to_seek_expert: Consult your local agronomy extension if leaf blighting accelerates during tuber bulking stage.

description: The notorious cause of the Irish Potato Famine, potato late blight can destroy whole crops in 7-10 days under cloudy, wet, cool weather.
symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked dark patches on leaf tips and margins.
White moldy mildew coating on the underside of infected leaves in moist mornings.
Brownish-black water-soaked lesions on stems.
Tubers show coppery-brown dry rot extending into flesh.
causes: Phytophthora infestans oomycete spores spread by wind and cool rainy gusts.
contributing_conditions: Temperatures between 12°C and 20°C with relative humidity above 90% for multiple consecutive days.
immediate_steps: Apply protective contact fungicides immediately across uninfected foliage if alert is active.
Cut and destroy haulms (potato vines) if blight is widespread, waiting 2 weeks before harvest to safeguard tubers.
organic_cultural_management: Preventive sprays of Bordeaux mixture (1%) or approved copper compounds.
Deep hilling of potato ridges (minimum 10-12 cm cover) to prevent spores washing into tubers.
prevention_methods: Plant resistant varieties (such as Kufri Girdhari, Kufri Jyoti where adapted).
Never leave discarded seed tubers in open cull piles.
safe_handling_precautions: Do not harvest when vines are wet or when soil is muddy.
when_to_seek_expert: Immediately alert local agricultural department officials for localized late blight spray forecast advisories.

description: The potato plant demonstrates healthy vegetative canopy growth, clean green leaflets, and vigorous stem architecture.
symptoms: Uniform green foliage with clean leaf margins.
Strong erect stems without dark streaking or wilting.
Normal flowering and tuber stolon development.
causes: Good soil aeration, certified seed tuber quality, and balanced nutrition.
contributing_conditions: Loose, friable sandy-loam soils with good drainage and pH 5.2 - 6.5.
immediate_steps: Continue scheduled earthing-up (hilling) around stems.
Maintain consistent soil moisture without waterlogging.
organic_cultural_management: Top-dress with decomposed farmyard manure or neem cake.
Maintain mulching to regulate soil temperature.
prevention_methods: Keep surveillance for aphid vectors and early leaf spot blemishes.
safe_handling_precautions: Store harvested seed tubers in cool, ventilated, diffused-light conditions.
when_to_seek_expert: No action needed. Continue standard agronomic practices.

description: Common rust is an airborne fungal disease of maize characterized by distinctive cinnamon-brown pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces.
symptoms: Small, elongated cinnamon-brown to reddish powdery pustules (uredinia) scattered on both leaf surfaces.
Pustules rupture the leaf epidermis, shedding powdery spores upon touch.
In late season, pustules turn brownish-black as winter teliospores develop.
Extensive chlorosis and leaf necrosis under heavy infection.
causes: Puccinia sorghi fungal spores carried over long distances by prevailing wind currents.
contributing_conditions: Cool to moderate temperatures (16°C to 25°C).
High relative humidity (>95%) and 6+ hours of dew formation.
immediate_steps: Inspect ear leaf and above; if rust is confined to lowest leaves near harvest, treatment may not be cost-effective.
If pustules appear on ear leaf before silking, consult local agronomy advisory for fungicide evaluation.
organic_cultural_management: Ensure optimal plant nutrition with balanced potassium to bolster plant cell wall defense.
prevention_methods: Plant rust-resistant or tolerant corn hybrids possessing the Rp resistance gene.
Plant early in the season to allow corn to mature before airborne spore flights peak.
safe_handling_precautions: Wear dust masks when walking through or harvesting heavily rusted fields.
when_to_seek_expert: Consult extension agronomists if rust pustules cover more than 10% of the upper canopy prior to blister stage (R2).

description: Northern corn leaf blight (NCLB) is a serious foliar disease producing large, cigar-shaped necrotic lesions that reduce photosynthetic capability and grain fill.
symptoms: Large, elongated, elliptical or cigar-shaped lesions (2.5 to 15 cm long).
Lesions start greyish-green and turn tan or brownish.
Dark olive or black fungal sporulation visible inside lesions in damp morning air.
Severe blighting resembles drought stress or frost damage.
causes: Exserohilum turcicum surviving on corn residue on soil surface.
contributing_conditions: Moderate temperatures (18°C to 27°C).
Extended wet spells, heavy morning dew, and overcast skies.
immediate_steps: Avoid overhead irrigation during humid periods.
Scout canopy weekly from whorl to tassel stage.
organic_cultural_management: Deep chisel plowing after harvest to bury infected corn residue.
Foliar spray of biocontrol agents like Trichoderma viride.
prevention_methods: Rotate with non-host crops (soybean, peanut, cotton, sorghum).
Select hybrids with single-gene (Ht genes) or polygenic resistance.
safe_handling_precautions: Clean combine harvesters and tillers after working in diseased fields.
when_to_seek_expert: Contact your district agricultural officer if lesions reach the ear leaf or above 2 weeks before or after tasseling.

description: The maize plant displays broad, arching dark green leaves, a thick healthy stalk, and normal tassel and silk emergence.
symptoms: Smooth, clean, broad green leaf blades without pustules or lesions.
Stout stalk without softening or discolored nodes.
Uniform tassel branch opening and vibrant silks.
causes: Optimal seed spacing, adequate basal fertilizer, and clean cultivation.
contributing_conditions: Warm growing weather (25°C - 32°C) with consistent moisture.
immediate_steps: Maintain adequate moisture during critical silking and tassel pollination stages.
Top-dress with nitrogen or organic compost at knee-high stage.
organic_cultural_management: Intercrop with legumes (cowpea, beans) to boost soil nitrogen.
Maintain shallow inter-row hoeing for weed management.
prevention_methods: Use certified high-germination seed stock.
Soil testing every two seasons.
safe_handling_precautions: General safe farming protocols.
when_to_seek_expert: No current action needed.

description: Bacterial leaf blight (BLB) of rice causes drying of leaves and 'kresek' (systemic seedling wilt), causing grain yield losses up to 50% in major Asian rice-growing belts.
symptoms: Water-soaked stripes along leaf margins turning yellow to bleached straw-white.
Wavy or undulated lesion margins.
Milky bacterial exudate droplets oozing on young lesions in early morning dew, drying into amber beads.
In young seedlings, systemic wilting and rolling of entire leaves ('Kresek' phase).
causes: Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae entering through hydathodes or mechanical clipping wounds.
contributing_conditions: High temperatures (25°C to 34°C) with high humidity (>70%).
Cyclones, strong winds, and flooding rains that create leaf abrasions.
Excessive nitrogen fertilizer application without balancing potassium.
immediate_steps: Drain standing field water temporarily for 3-4 days to arrest bacterial multiplication.
Halt top-dressing nitrogen fertilizers immediately.
Apply potassium muriate (potash) to strengthen plant epidermal silica layers.
organic_cultural_management: Spray 20% fresh cow dung water extract or neem oil (3%) after filtering.
Apply bio-agents like Pseudomonas fluorescens at 10g/L.
prevention_methods: Plant resistant varieties (e.g., Improved Samba Mahsuri, Swarna-Sub1, IR64).
Do not clip seedling leaf tips at transplanting (creates entry wounds).
Keep field bunds clear of weed hosts like Leersia and wild rice.
safe_handling_precautions: Avoid walking in wet paddy fields during active blight outbreak.
when_to_seek_expert: Seek guidance from your local Agricultural Assistant or KVK regarding certified bactericide formulations and drainage timing.

description: Rice brown spot is a notorious chronic fungal disease linked historically to poor soil fertility and water stress, damaging both foliage and panicle grains.
symptoms: Small, circular to oval sesame-seed shaped brown spots with yellow halos.
Older spots have grey or whitish centers with dark brown borders.
Dark brown to black discoloration on glumes (grain husks) causing unfilled or chaffy grains.
Reduced milling quality and dark spotting on milled rice kernel.
causes: Fungal pathogen Bipolaris oryzae surviving in seed and soil stubble.
contributing_conditions: Nutrient-deficient soils (especially deficient in silicon, manganese, potassium, or nitrogen).
Drought stress or intermittent water deficit in rainfed lowlands.
immediate_steps: Restore proper irrigation depth (3-5 cm standing water) to relieve drought stress.
Apply light balanced nutrient top-dressing including micronutrients.
organic_cultural_management: Seed treatment with Pseudomonas fluorescens (10 g/kg seed) before sowing.
Foliar spray of neem seed extract or compost tea.
prevention_methods: Conduct soil test and amend sandy or degraded soils with organic farmyard manure.
Use certified clean seeds; hot water soak seeds at 52°C-54°C for 10-15 minutes.
Apply balanced NPK with supplemental zinc and silica.
safe_handling_precautions: Ensure proper drying of harvested paddy grains below 14% moisture before storage.
when_to_seek_expert: Consult your agricultural university extension if spots cover more than 20% of flag leaf area before panicle emergence.

description: The paddy plant exhibits vibrant green tillering, healthy erect flag leaves, and clean glumes on developing panicles.
symptoms: Upright, deep green leaf blades without spots, discolored margins, or bacterial beads.
Stout tillers firmly anchored in puddle soil.
Clean, golden-tinted emergent panicles.
causes: System of Rice Intensification (SRI) or balanced puddling, proper water level, and balanced fertilization.
contributing_conditions: Sunny tropical days with well-regulated water regime.
immediate_steps: Maintain recommended water depth according to growth stage (shallow during tillering, saturated at flowering).
organic_cultural_management: Incorporate green manure crops (dhaincha or sunn hemp) during puddling.
Release Trichogramma egg parasitoids for stem borer biocontrol.
prevention_methods: Maintain clean field bunds and ensure alternate wetting and drying (AWD) water management.
safe_handling_precautions: General paddy field maintenance.
when_to_seek_expert: No intervention needed.

description: Bacterial spot on bell peppers and chillies causes severe defoliation, blossom drop, and unsightly blistered spots on peppers, drastically reducing market value.
symptoms: Small, yellow-green spots on young leaves that turn dark brown and water-soaked.
Spots often cluster along leaf margins or tips where water droplets collect.
Extensive leaf yellowing followed by severe defoliation, exposing fruits to sunscald.
Rough, elevated, wart-like brown scabs on pepper pods.
causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria transmitted via infected seed and rain splash.
contributing_conditions: Temperatures between 24°C and 30°C.
Frequent rain showers and overhead sprinkler systems.
immediate_steps: Stop overhead sprinkling; shift to drip lines immediately.
Avoid handling pepper plants while foliage is damp.
organic_cultural_management: Apply approved copper hydroxide or bio-fungicide like Bacillus subtilis according to label directions.
Apply organic straw mulch around plant bases.
prevention_methods: Plant certified disease-free bell pepper / chilli seed varieties.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 2-3 years.
safe_handling_precautions: Sterilize pruning tools and trays with alcohol or bleach solution between crops.
when_to_seek_expert: Seek guidance from your horticulture extension agent if copper-resistant strains are reported in your area.

description: The pepper plant exhibits vigorous dark green foliage, healthy branching, and robust flower and pod formation without blemishes.
symptoms: Glossy, smooth, deep green leaves without blemishes or marginal scorch.
Sturdy woody main stem and healthy branching nodes.
Glossy, firm, spotless fruit developing uniformly.
causes: Balanced soil nutrients, calcium availability, and regular moisture.
contributing_conditions: Warm days (22°C - 30°C), well-drained loamy soil with organic matter.
immediate_steps: Maintain steady drip irrigation to prevent blossom-end rot.
Inspect undersides of leaves for mites and thrips.
organic_cultural_management: Apply foliar neem oil spray once every 14 days.
Top-dress with vermicompost and bone meal for phosphorus.
prevention_methods: Ensure proper plant spacing (45-60 cm) for air flow.
safe_handling_precautions: Standard farming hygiene.
when_to_seek_expert: No current action needed.

description: Apple scab is the most economically significant disease of apples worldwide, causing olive-green velvety lesions on leaves and severely deformed, cracked fruit.
symptoms: Olive-green to velvety dark brown circular spots on leaf surfaces.
Leaves become distorted, puckered, and may drop prematurely.
Scabby, corky, dark brown or black lesions on fruit skin that may crack open, allowing secondary rot.
causes: Venturia inaequalis fungus overwintering in fallen leaves on the orchard floor.
contributing_conditions: Cool, rainy spring weather with temperatures between 15°C and 24°C.
Prolonged leaf wetness spanning 9 to 18 continuous hours.
immediate_steps: Prune overcrowded inner branches during dormancy to improve air circulation and canopy drying.
Rake and destroy or shred fallen orchard leaves in autumn to eliminate overwintering ascocarps.
organic_cultural_management: Apply sulfur or lime sulfur sprays during green tip through petal fall according to organic orchard spray schedules.
Spray 5% urea solution on fallen autumn leaves to accelerate leaf breakdown before spring spore release.
prevention_methods: Plant scab-resistant cultivars (e.g., Liberty, Prima, Enterprise, GoldRush).
Monitor Mills infection period chart to time protective sprays accurately.
safe_handling_precautions: Wear eye protection and respirator when applying orchard sulfur formulations.
when_to_seek_expert: Consult your regional fruit research station or horticulture officer for local Mills infection alerts and fungicide resistance management.

description: Apple black rot affects leaves (frog-eye leaf spot), branches (cankers), and fruit, causing mummified fruit and limb dieback in orchards.
symptoms: Small purple spots on leaves expanding into circular lesions with light brown centers and dark purple borders ('frog-eye' appearance).
Firm brown rot on fruit starting near calyx, showing concentric light and dark brown rings.
Infected fruit turns into hard, shriveled black mummies adhering to twigs.
Sunken, reddish-brown bark cankers on limbs.
causes: Botryosphaeria obtusa fungus surviving in dead wood, prunings, and mummified apples.
contributing_conditions: Warm, humid weather (24°C to 28°C) accompanied by frequent rains.
Pre-existing tree wounds from insect feeding, hail, fire blight, or winter freeze.
immediate_steps: Prune out dead branches, twigs, and cankers at least 15 cm below visible margins.
Knock down and destroy all mummified fruits left hanging on trees.
organic_cultural_management: Apply protective copper or captan fungicides during early fruit development per orchard advisory.
Paint large pruning cuts with tree wound sealers or sanitized white latex paint.
prevention_methods: Keep trees vigorously nourished and avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen.
Control insect pests (codling moth, plum curculio) that create fruit entry punctures.
safe_handling_precautions: Sterilize pruning loppers between cuts with 70% alcohol.
when_to_seek_expert: Consult orchard extension officers if large scaffold limb cankers threaten tree structure.

description: A heteroecious rust fungus requiring both apple/crabapple trees and eastern red cedar / juniper trees to complete its two-year lifecycle.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange or fiery red spots on upper leaf surfaces in late spring.
Tiny black specks (pycnia) develop inside the orange spots.
Tube-like finger structures (aecia) erupt on the underside of leaves and fruit.
Premature leaf yellowing and defoliation.
causes: Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae spores discharged from gelatinous cedar galls during warm spring rains.
contributing_conditions: Presence of juniper or red cedar trees within 1-2 km of apple orchard.
Spring temperatures between 10°C and 24°C with moist rainfall.
immediate_steps: Remove nearby wild red cedar or ornamental juniper trees within 500 meters of the orchard where feasible.
Prune out visible brown cedar-apple galls on nearby junipers in winter.
organic_cultural_management: Apply sulfur-based protective sprays at tight cluster through petal fall stages.
Apply preventative myclobutanil or mancozeb per local extension spray calendar.
prevention_methods: Plant rust-immune or resistant apple cultivars (e.g., Redfree, Freedom, Liberty, William's Pride).
Avoid planting susceptible varieties (Honeycrisp, Rome, Golden Delicious) near cedar shelterbelts.
safe_handling_precautions: Follow standard spray drift safety measures.
when_to_seek_expert: Consult local fruit extension specialists if defoliation exceeds 20% in consecutive years.

description: The apple tree showcases healthy green foliage, clean spur development, and normal fruit set without blemishes or rust spots.
symptoms: Bright, glossy green ovate leaves without velvety patches or orange spots.
Firm, clean fruitlets without cracks or russeting.
Smooth bark and vigorous terminal shoot extension.
causes: Proper winter pruning, orchard floor sanitation, and integrated pest management.
contributing_conditions: Temperate climate with adequate winter chilling hours and full sun.
immediate_steps: Maintain balanced orchard irrigation and clean tree ring basins.
Thin excess fruitlets to encourage uniform size and prevent limb breakage.
organic_cultural_management: Apply composted mulch around the drip line.
Maintain pheromone traps for codling moth monitoring.
prevention_methods: Conduct dormant winter lime sulfur sprays.
safe_handling_precautions: Sanitize pruning equipment before winter pruning.
when_to_seek_expert: No action needed.

description: Black rot is one of the most destructive diseases of cultivated grapes, causing berry shriveling into hard, black, wrinkled mummies and circular leaf spots.
symptoms: Small circular reddish-brown leaf spots with distinct dark brown margins.
Tiny black pimples (pycnidia) arranged in a ring inside leaf spots.
Infected berries turn pale, then soft and sunken, before shriveling into hard black mummies covered with pycnidia.
Dark elongated lesions on young shoots and petioles.
causes: Guignardia bidwellii fungus overwintering in mummified berries left on trellises or vineyard floor.
contributing_conditions: Warm, wet weather (20°C to 27°C) requiring 6-12 hours of continuous vine wetness.
Dense canopy with poor air movement and shaded vine interiors.
immediate_steps: Prune and destroy all mummified grape clusters still clinging to vines.
Canopy shoot positioning and leaf pulling around fruit clusters to accelerate morning sun drying.
organic_cultural_management: Apply protective copper or mancozeb sprays starting at 2-inch shoot growth through 4 weeks post-bloom.
Cultivate or bury vineyard floor debris before bud break in spring.
prevention_methods: Train vines on high trellis systems for enhanced air circulation.
Select resistant grape cultivars where suited (e.g., Norton, Chancellor).
safe_handling_precautions: Disinfect pruning shears with alcohol between vine blocks.
when_to_seek_expert: Consult your viticulture extension specialist if black rot appears on clusters during early fruit set.

description: Esca is a destructive grapevine trunk disease complex affecting mature vineyards, causing 'tiger-stripe' leaf necrosis, spotted berries, and sudden apoplexy (vine collapse).
symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' chlorotic and necrotic patterns between leaf veins.
Small, dark purplish-brown spots on berries known as 'black measles'.
Internal trunk cross-section shows brown wood streaking and soft yellow spongy decay.
Sudden apoplexy: rapid wilting and collapse of entire vines during hot dry spells.
causes: Complex of vascular and wood-rotting fungal pathogens entering through winter pruning wounds.
contributing_conditions: Older vines (typically >8-10 years).
Large pruning wounds made during wet winter weather.
Severe water stress following hot summer temperature spikes.
immediate_steps: Mark symptomatic vines with bright tape during summer for remedial winter trunk surgery.
Avoid water stress by maintaining uniform drip irrigation.
organic_cultural_management: Apply Trichoderma-based pruning wound protectant paste immediately after winter trimming.
Prune vines late in the dormant season (just before bud break) when wound healing is fastest.
prevention_methods: Practice clean pruning: make clean, smooth cuts without ripping vine bark.
Never prune vines during rain or when canopy is dripping.
safe_handling_precautions: Remove dead trunk sections from the vineyard and burn or incinerate them.
when_to_seek_expert: Consult a viticulturist for trunk renewal (retraining water sprouts from ground) or graft replacement techniques.

description: Isariopsis leaf spot or grape leaf blight causes premature defoliation in late summer, exposing clusters to sunburn and diminishing cold hardiness.
symptoms: Irregular brown to reddish-brown necrotic spots with faint yellowish margins.
Olive-colored velvety mold visible on the underside of leaf lesions.
Spots coalesce into extensive blighted sectors causing leaf curling and dropping.
Reduced sugar accumulation and delayed berry ripening.
causes: Pseudocercospora fungal spores spread by wind and rain splash.
contributing_conditions: Warm temperatures (22°C to 28°C) accompanied by high relative humidity.
Crowded vine canopies with poor sunlight penetration.
immediate_steps: Carry out leaf thinning in the fruiting zone to facilitate fast drying.
Ensure proper vineyard drainage to prevent stagnant moisture.
organic_cultural_management: Apply Bordeaux mixture (1%) or copper oxychloride per regional viticulture advisory.
Maintain vineyard floor clean of weed clusters.
prevention_methods: Regular trellis maintenance to prevent sprawling canes.
Post-harvest copper wash before winter dormancy.
safe_handling_precautions: Use appropriate protective gear when spraying copper fungicides.
when_to_seek_expert: Consult your local horticulture department if severe defoliation occurs before veraison.

description: The grapevine demonstrates vigorous shoot elongation, clean glossy green leaves, and well-distributed uniform fruit clusters.
symptoms: Expansive, vibrant green palmate leaves without marginal scorch or spots.
Robust green shoots with active tendrils.
Clean, bloom-covered grape berries developing evenly.
causes: Optimal winter spur pruning, canopy management, and micro-irrigation.
contributing_conditions: Full sunshine, well-drained rocky or gravelly loam, and good ventilation.
immediate_steps: Maintain regular canopy shoot tucking into trellis wires.
Monitor soil moisture with tensiometers.
organic_cultural_management: Mulch under-vine strip with composted vineyard pomace.
Maintain beneficial insect flowering borders.
prevention_methods: Routine scouting for powdery mildew and berry moth.
safe_handling_precautions: Standard viticultural best practices.
when_to_seek_expert: No intervention required.
